about.title: About Read TES
about.intro: Read TES is an independent, interactive reading of Talmud Eser Sefirot — Baal HaSulam's foundational commentary on the Kabbalah of the Ari — built by students of Bnei Baruch Kabbalah Academy for anyone studying the text closely. The text is in Hebrew and English, with Bnei Baruch translations of some parts in Russian, Ukrainian, Spanish, and French; the interface is available in nine languages.
about.readingModelBody: The reader follows the structure of Talmud Eser Sefirot itself: the Ari's numbered text, Baal HaSulam's Inner Light explanation anchored directly to it, and Inner Observation as the deeper systematic explanation for the part. Inner Observation is continuous rather than paragraph-linked, so it remains an independent reading pane.

glossary.title: Glossary
glossary.lede: {count} terms of Talmud Eser Sefirot, and the English the official edition actually uses for each one.
glossary.evidence: Every term here was read off the {chapters} chapters where the 1956 Jerusalem Hebrew and the Bnei Baruch English could be laid side by side, item against item — {items} aligned pairs in all.
glossary.languageNote: The Hebrew is quoted from the 1956 Jerusalem edition and the English from the Bnei Baruch edition. The short notes are shown in your interface language.
glossary.coverageStripDescription: The English edition covers parts {parts} of the sixteen parts of Talmud Eser Sefirot.
glossary.strategyFilterLabel: Filter by how the term crosses into English
glossary.attestedNowhere: Not attested in any aligned part.
glossary.variantsHint: Counts are occurrences inside the aligned passages, not across the whole book.
glossary.citationsFailed: The passages could not be loaded.
glossary.emptyBody: Try another spelling, in Hebrew or English — quotation marks inside acronyms are ignored.
glossary.conventionsIntro: Rules the official edition follows beyond single words — how item markers, commentary openings, citations and honorifics are handled — each with passages as examples.
glossary.limitsIntro: This glossary is only as wide as the English edition. Read these before leaning on a count.
glossary.methodBody: Wherever the Hebrew (Jerusalem edition) and the official Bnei Baruch English both exist for the same chapter and layer, the two were laid side by side and matched item for item; a match was accepted only when the numbering and anchors lined up exactly. For each Hebrew term, the English renderings that turn up unusually often in the items containing it were gathered as candidates, and every candidate was then confirmed by reading real pairs. Every quoted passage was pulled out of the matched text by program, not typed by hand.

noteCopy.or: Never transliterated as Ohr. Capitalised only inside the section names “Inner Light” and “Inner Observation.”
noteCopy.kli: Translated, not transliterated. “Kli” occurs once in the whole English corpus.
noteCopy.zakut: Also rendered as “refinement,” like הזדככות; see the inconsistencies.
noteCopy.reshimo: Always translated. “Reshimo” and “Reshimot” never appear in the official English.
noteCopy.zivug: Hebrew is spelled זווג throughout this corpus; זיווג does not occur.
noteCopy.histaklut-pnimit: The name of Baal HaSulam’s second commentary layer. Both words are capitalised.
noteCopy.histaklut: As a technical term for Malchut looking at the light, this is “a look” or “looking,” not “observation.”
noteCopy.or-pnimi: Two senses: the title of Baal HaSulam’s first commentary layer, and the lower-case technical term.
noteCopy.behina: The edition reserves “discernment” for הבחן or הבחנה, not בחינה as a level.
noteCopy.behina-dalet: Phase ordinals are written as words: phase one, two, three and four.
noteCopy.madrega: קומה is “level”; מדרגה is “degree.” Both can occur together.
noteCopy.atzmut: עצמותו ית׳ is “His self.” “Essence” is reserved for מהות.
noteCopy.nekudot: The official English genuinely varies here; see the inconsistencies.
noteCopy.partzufim: The first occurrence in an item is glossed “Partzufim [pl. of Partzuf].”
noteCopy.toch: Transliterated only for the technical middle third of a Partzuf; ordinary תוך or בתוך is “inside” or “within.”
noteCopy.sof: Distinct from אין סוף, “Ein Sof.” Glossed “[end]” or “[end/conclusion]” on first use.
noteCopy.ein-sof: א״ס ב״ה is “Ein Sof”; the ב״ה honorific is omitted.
noteCopy.atzilut: The world is “Atzilut”; the act of emanating is lower-case “emanation.”
noteCopy.adam-kadmon: Spelled out in Parts 1–2 and abbreviated “AK” from Part 3 onward.
noteCopy.hochma: “Wisdom” is used only in the phrase “wisdom of Kabbalah.”
noteCopy.bon: BON, not BAN. Paired as “MA and BON.”
noteCopy.za: Spelled out in Parts 1–3 and abbreviated from Part 5 onward.
noteCopy.einayim: The official English genuinely varies here; see the inconsistencies.
noteCopy.klipot: Usually translated as “shells”; once transliterated as “Klipot [shells].”
noteCopy.harav: In TES הרב denotes the ARI, and the official English always renders it “the ARI,” never “the Rav.”
noteCopy.akudim: Always capitalised: “world of Akudim,” “Keter of Akudim.”
noteCopy.ohr-hozer-abbrev: The abbreviation uses the same rendering as אור חוזר; it is never “Ohr Hozer.”
noteCopy.ohr-yashar-abbrev: Matches אור ישר. Added in version 2 and absent from version 1.
noteCopy.bitushim-plural: Derived from the fixed singular ביטוש: clash. Unattested; flag any use for review.

limits.coverage: The Bnei Baruch English covers only parts {parts} of the sixteen. For the other parts, no term is evidenced here.
limits.runningProse: Most of the evidence comes from the Tables of Questions and Answers, which are terminological by nature. Only a handful of running chapters could be compared, so what the glossary shows about prose style is thinner than what it shows about single terms.
limits.thinTerms: A few terms occur in only one to three compared passages. That is too little to settle them, so they are left out rather than guessed.
limits.wholeChapters: A few chapters could be compared only as a whole, not item by item, so passages quoted from them are weaker evidence.
limits.aiNotUsed: The AI English translation on this site was not used to build the glossary; it was only checked against the finished glossary.

item-markers-gematria.rule: A Hebrew letter used as an inline marker is written as its numerical value in Arabic numerals (gematria): aleph is 1, yod is 10, lamed is 30, qof is 100, tav is 400. The letter itself is never kept, and markers are never renumbered in sequence.

commentary-lemma.rule: Each English commentary item opens with a bold lemma — the phrase from the source it comments on — followed by a colon, and then the explanation. The Hebrew commentary has no lemma and is identified only by its anchor, so a translation has to draw the lemma from the aligned source text.

nav-links-dropped.rule: The Hebrew links that lead from a question to its answer and back (“to the question”, “to the answer”) are dropped entirely. They have no English rendering.

answer-headword-dropped.rule: The bold Hebrew headword that opens an answer is not repeated in English; the item starts directly with the definition. A citation that follows the headword is moved to the end of the item or dropped, never left at the start.

question-punctuation.rule: Hebrew questions end with a full stop; the English edition writes them as questions ending in a question mark. When a citation is appended, the question mark is usually dropped and the item ends with the closing parenthesis.

abbreviation-expansion.rule: Hebrew abbreviations in citations are written out in English, never transliterated: part and chapter references become “Part 3, Chapter 5”, the two commentary layers are named in full as “Inner Light” and “Inner Observation”, and “item”, “page” and “see answer” take Arabic numerals. Back-references become “ibid.” or “see above item”. Every Hebrew letter-numeral becomes an Arabic numeral.

honorifics-dropped.rule: “Blessed be He” after Ein Sof is always dropped, so “Ein Sof” stands alone. The honorific on the Creator’s name is dropped or absorbed into “His” and “Him”. The Hebrew idiom for “God forbid” becomes the adverb “whatsoever” in negative clauses, or is dropped, and is never rendered “God forbid”. “See there” is usually dropped.

harav-is-ari.rule: In this text the Hebrew “the Rav” means the Ari (Isaac Luria), author of the Etz Chaim text being quoted. The English always says “the ARI” and never “the Rav”. Baal HaSulam, the commentator, is not named in the running text.

gloss-brackets.rule: A transliterated term is followed by a short English gloss in square brackets the first time it appears in an item, and is then used bare: “Rosh [head]”, “Guf [body]”, “Ein Sof [infinity]”, “Katnut [smallness]”, “Gadlut [greatness]”. The gloss is used sparingly, not on every occurrence.

phase-ordinals.rule: Phase ordinals are spelled as words in lower case — “phase one”, “phase two”, “phase three”, “phase four” — and never as digits. In the same way “ten Sefirot” keeps “ten” as a lower-case word.

feminine-malchut.rule: Malchut, phase four and the Nukva keep their Hebrew feminine grammar in English: “she”, “her”, “herself”. They are never turned into “it”.

typography.rule: Quoted terms use curly typographic quotes, never straight ASCII quotes, and glosses use square brackets. Hebrew letters appear in the English only inside letter glosses.

layer-names.rule: “Inner Light”, the name of Baal HaSulam’s first commentary layer, is written in title case; the same words in lower case, “inner light”, are the technical term for light clothed inside a vessel. “Inner Observation” names the second layer. The difference in case is the only thing that tells the layer name from the term.
